strengths: The practical contribution supports weak acceptance. MaskSub combines supervised training on unmasked inputs with self-distillation onto masked inputs using shared parameters. The objective is coherent, implementation is simple, and inference cost is unchanged.

The core ImageNet evidence is convincing. Table 1 reports gains of 0.6–0.7 percentage points across four ViT sizes at 400 epochs. Table A.13 provides repeated-run support: ViT-B improves from 83.46 ± 0.04 to 84.08 ± 0.02. Improvements also extend to ResNet, Swin, and several pretrained-model fine-tuning recipes.

Training-budget comparisons substantiate practical efficiency. In Table 8, ViT-B reaches 84.1% using 25 GPU days versus 83.7% using 26 GPU days for longer baseline training. Table 9 also shows higher accuracy than CoSub with less computation. These controls strengthen attribution beyond comparisons at equal epoch counts.

Evaluation extends meaningfully beyond ImageNet classification. Table 10 reports ADE20K improvements, Table A.3 includes detection and instance segmentation, and Table A.4 shows consistent robustness gains across model sizes and benchmarks. For example, ViT-H ImageNet-A accuracy rises from 51.9% to 58.3%.

The appendix contains useful ablations and reproducibility details. Table A.6 supports the importance of distillation: ViT-B achieves 83.6% without KD versus 84.1% with it. Mask-ratio and loss-weight sweeps, repeated runs for several experiments, Algorithm 1, detailed training recipes, and a code link make the central method reasonably reproducible.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is modest. The method combines established masking and asymmetric self-distillation. Section 2's distinction between its distillation loss and prior consistency learning is overstated: with detached teacher predictions, Equation 3 has the same student gradient as KL consistency. The contribution is chiefly the effective supervised-training application and its empirical validation.

The explanation of automatic difficulty control exceeds the evidence. Figures 2 and A.1 demonstrate useful loss and gradient trends, but do not establish selective regularization of successfully learned examples. Every example receives the masked-branch objective, and a confidently incorrect teacher can supply a strong erroneous target. The empirical optimization benefit is better supported than the proposed sample-wise mechanism.

Benefits are not universal, despite broad headline claims. In Table A.10, adding MaskSub during ViT-B fine-tuning reduces CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.89% to 89.55%. Section 4.2 also acknowledges that CLIP's best checkpoint does not improve; its reported advantage concerns final-epoch performance. These exceptions limit the claim of consistently beneficial use without task-specific adjustment.

Some secondary results have weaker statistical or computational controls. The 0.1-point BEiTv2 improvements and 0.2/0.3-point COCO AP improvements lack reported run variability, while CLIP pretraining lacks a comparable-budget baseline. Furthermore, the approximately 1.5× training cost depends on token removal; Section 4.3 reports doubled computation for hierarchical architectures.

Minor presentation issues are readily correctable: Table 7 labels both CIFAR columns as CIFAR100, and Section 4's statement that all experiments use 50% masking conflicts with the 15% BERT setting. These issues do not determine the recommendation; the substantive reservations concern novelty, mechanism, and the scope of the claims.
